ideas.name: long-travel geared prismatic jaw
ideas.description: The servo horn drives a 25-tooth printed gear meshing with a 50-tooth gear on a second shaft on two MR63 bearings. That shaft carries a module-1 50-tooth pinion (25 mm pitch radius) that drives a rack on a carriage on two LM3UU bushings riding 3 x 150 mm steel rods. The finger slides straight along the closing axis at ~50 mm per servo radian (about 106 mm max opening, ~10 mm min). Its face stays vertical and parallel, and its tip stays level with the fixed jaw at every width.
ideas.test: Add a prismatic jaw variant with effective pitch radius 50 mm (gear ratio 2 x 25 mm pinion), carriage travel ~96 mm on 150 mm rods, squeeze = stall torque / 0.05 m with gear efficiency ~0.9, and the extra wrist mass (~45 g). Re-run all 21 groups, especially dice (17 mm) and the gear-reduced position resolution at small openings.

ideas.name: stepped-up rack jaw on 100 mm rods
ideas.description: A carriage slides on two 3x100 mm steel rods, one LM3UU bushing per rod, and holds the moving finger with its face vertical and parallel to the fixed jaw. A printed module-1 rack on the carriage is driven by a 46-tooth pinion on an idler shaft (a cut 3 mm rod in two MR63 bearings). A printed 40:20 spur pair from the servo horn steps the speed up 2:1, so the servo's 1.92 rad turns the pinion 3.84 rad: 88 mm of straight stroke, a 14 to 102 mm opening, and about 35 N of squeeze. The fingertip neither turns nor rises, so it reaches the side of a box 38 mm tall at 90 mm, where the hinge leaves it 28 to 31 mm high. Keep the existing TPU pads with pad_angle_deg=0, and add a groove of about 2 mm for spheres.
ideas.test: A prismatic jaw whose finger travels 46 mm per servo radian (23 mm pinion pitch radius x 2:1 gear), with an 88 mm stroke (opening 14 to 102 mm) and squeeze = servo torque / 0.046 m less about 10% gear loss, plus about 70 g at the wrist. Pads at pad_angle_deg=0 with groove_mm of about 2. Run all 21 objects, especially pudding, sugar, mustard and tuna, and the round held ones (golf_ball, racquetball, apple, tennis_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, tomato_soup_can) and dice at the narrow end.

ideas.name: phase-offset parallelogram jaw (links leaning toward closing at the closed position)
ideas.description: A four-bar parallelogram carries the moving finger without turning it, as the catalogue part does. The difference is that the servo horn and both links are indexed so the links lean about 0.42 rad toward the fixed jaw when the jaw is closed. As the servo opens the jaw, the finger's arc of radius 95 mm passes through its lowest point near the middle of the range rather than starting there. The tip height then varies by only about -8/+7 mm over the whole 8 to 100 mm opening, where the stock hinge rises +28 mm by 85 mm. Because the face stays vertical, both contacts stay horizontal and opposed, and the moving pad is printed at 0 deg tilt. The servo sweep is about 1.0 rad, and squeeze is 17 to 21 N.
ideas.test: Add a phase_rad parameter (range 0 to 0.6 rad, the link lean at the closed position) to the parallelogram jaw builder. The servo zero is indexed by that offset, and the opening and tip height come from 95 cos(θ) and 95 sin(θ) across the sweep from -phase_rad to the servo limit. Run it with link_mm=95, phase_rad=0.42 and the pad's tilt at 0 deg. Check the table-clearance dip for the 42 to 59 mm objects first.

ideas.name: slotted-lever (Scotch-yoke) straight-line jaw
ideas.description: The stock jaw servo turns a printed slotted lever about the existing hinge axis. A pin on the moving-pad carriage, fitted with an MR63 bearing as a roller, rides in the lever's slot. The carriage slides in a printed dovetail track fixed to the gripper body, running along the closing axis at fingertip height (h = 81 mm below the hinge axis). The carriage only translates, x = h*tan(q), so the moving face stays parallel to the fixed face and the moving tip stays level with the fixed tip at every opening from 0 to about 100 mm. Squeeze is servo torque*cos^2(q)/h, which is 20 N near closed and about 9.5 N fully open. A second MR63 on the carriage's track side cuts sliding friction. The pads keep a TPU skin with pad_angle 0. Unlike the recorded geared and rack ideas, it needs no rods, no gear stage and no new purchases beyond two bearings.
ideas.test: A jaw type 'slotted_yoke' with parameter h_mm in [60, 100]. The moving finger is a prismatic joint along the closing axis, coupled to the servo angle by x = h*tan(q - q0) (equality/tendon coupling, or a pin-in-slot contact pair), with the face kept at 0 deg and the tip at the fixed tip's height. Squeeze is limited to servo torque*cos^2(q)/h. Wrist mass is about 35 g extra.

ideas.name: offset fixed finger with a self-aligning pivot pad on the moving jaw
ideas.description: 1) A reprinted fixed jaw (gripper base) whose vertical face sits 20 mm farther from the moving jaw, at the same height. The stock fixed jaw is part of the gripper body, so the base is reprinted rather than given a bolt-on spacer, which would leave the old face in the way. The gripper servo and hinge are reused unchanged. The arc's lowest point moves from a 25 mm to a 45 mm opening. From 17 to 96 mm the fingertip then stays within 5-18 mm of the fixed tip, compared with up to +28 mm at 85 mm now (and 90-96 mm out of reach). 2) The moving pad is replaced by a TPU-skinned pad on an M3 pivot pin running in two MR63 bearings, with printed stops at ±40 deg and a light return spring. It seats flush on flat sides at any jaw angle, so the contact normal stays horizontal and antipodal to the fixed face. The fixed pad stays as it is now (TPU, 12 mm wide).

ideas.name: full-turn rack jaw (prismatic jaw with the gripper servo's position range widened to about 205 deg)
ideas.description: A printed 48-tooth module-1 pinion (50 mm across) on the gripper servo horn drives a printed rack on a carriage. The carriage rides two 3 x 100 mm steel rods on one LM3UU bushing per rod. The fixed finger sits on the frame just past the far end of the rods. The STS3215 angle limits (min/max angle registers) are widened from about 110 deg to about 205 deg of its 360-deg, 4096-step range. Travel is 24 mm per rad × 3.5 rad ≈ 84 mm, so the opening runs from about 14 to 98 mm. The finger neither turns nor rises (the catalogue prismatic shows +2 mm at every width), so the pad stays parallel to the fixed face and reaches below the top of the 34 to 58 mm-tall wide objects. The TPU pads are kept with pad_angle_deg=0. Squeeze is servo torque over the 24 mm pitch radius: up to about 67 N, set lower by the close target. Sugar at 514 g needs only 2·0.5·N > 7.6 N.
ideas.test: Use the existing prismatic jaw builder with two changes: pinion_teeth=48 (beyond its current 17-60 sampling is fine), and the gripper joint range raised from -0.17..1.75 to -0.17..3.6 rad, with carriage travel capped at 84 mm by the 100 mm rods. Set pads to pad_angle_deg=0, pad_tpu_mm=2. Run all 21 objects, and check the 17 mm dice/marker at the low end and the 96 mm mustard at the top.

ideas.name: squeeze-locked drop finger on a parallelogram jaw
ideas.description: Start from the catalogue parallelogram jaw (link_mm 90, pad_angle_deg 0) so the moving face stays vertical at every opening. On its carriage, the finger is no longer rigid: it rides a vertical slot on two M3 screw pins (about 60 mm of travel, telescoping in two stages). With no load, the finger drops under its own weight until a low-friction PLA foot rests on the table, so the tip stays at table level however much the carriage rises (+49 mm at 85 mm). The slot's load-bearing wall is lined with TPU. Once the jaw clamps, the 20-37 N squeeze presses the pins against the lining and locks the slide by friction, so on lift the finger rises with the carriage. The face is TPU-skinned (0.9). The finger face sits 3-4 mm outboard so the opening reaches about 100 mm.
ideas.test: In the simulator, give the parallelogram finger a child body on a vertical slide joint (0 to 60 mm, gravity-driven), with a foot geom that collides with the table. Model the squeeze lock as slide friction proportional to the jaw's normal load (or a contact pair between the pin and a TPU-friction slot wall). Then run all 21 objects, checking the 17-19 mm small objects and the 84 mm potted_meat_can for collisions between the retracted finger and the wrist.

ideas.name: sector-gear rack jaw (long-radius printed gear segment on the catalogue's rod-and-carriage slide)
ideas.description: The catalogue prismatic jaw with its full pinion replaced by a printed module-1 gear SEGMENT of 42 mm pitch radius (84-tooth equivalent, ~30 teeth over ~120 deg) bolted to the gripper servo horn. It meshes a printed rack on a carriage that rides two 3x100 mm ground rods in LM3UU bushings. The finger slides straight along the closing axis, so its face never turns and its tip never rises (as with the catalogue prismatic, tip +2 mm). Because only the swept arc carries teeth, the radius is no longer capped by full-pinion clearance (60 teeth). Travel is 42 mm/rad x 1.92 rad = 81 mm, opening about 15-96 mm at 39 N squeeze. The pads move over unchanged except pad_angle_deg = 0.
ideas.test: A simulator builder for the prismatic jaw that accepts a non-integer or sector pitch radius up to 42 mm (equivalently pinion_teeth up to 84 with a sector-clearance check instead of a full-circle check), with the pads slot at pad_angle_deg=0. Run all 21 groups, especially dice/large_marker at the closed end and pudding/sugar/tuna/mustard at the open end.

ideas.name: geared symmetric twin-hinge jaw (both jaws swing, 2:1 reduction to each)
ideas.description: The stock fixed jaw is replaced by a printed hinged jaw that mirrors the moving one, pivoting on two MR63 bearings in a printed bracket on the gripper body. The stock moving jaw gets a matching pair of MR63 bearings and a printed gear rim. A printed spur gear on the gripper servo horn drives both jaw gears in opposite directions at 2:1, so each jaw turns half the servo angle. The existing TPU pads (pad_tpu 2 mm, friction 0.9) go on both jaws. pad_angle sets where both faces are parallel, aimed at about a 55 to 60 mm opening, so the faces tilt symmetrically within about ±15 deg across 17 to 105 mm. Because both tips rise equally and only a few mm, both reach below the top of short wide objects (tuna 34, pudding 38, sugar 45, mustard 58 mm tall) and hold the vertical sides antipodally. The opening comes from two half-swings, so it exceeds the 96 mm mustard width. Added wrist mass is about 25 g, which is small next to the 0.15 N*m per 100 g budget at the shoulder.
ideas.test: A jaw builder for a symmetric twin-hinge jaw: two revolute fingers, each 81 mm from its axis to its fingertip, mirrored about the gripper centreline and coupled by a gear constraint at -1:1 with each other and 1:2 to the gripper servo. Each finger takes the existing pads part (pad_angle applied symmetrically). The descent stops when the lower of the two fingertips reaches table clearance, and the fixed-jaw-face assumption in the contact checks has to be replaced by the second hinged face. Then run all 21 groups, especially dice (17 mm, each face about -15 deg bottom-in) and potted_meat_can (squeeze check at 20 N).

ideas.name: long-radius revolute jaw (pivot raised to about 160 mm above the tip, linkage-driven at 2:1)
ideas.description: The moving finger is a single rigid printed jaw about 160 mm long. It pivots on two MR63 bearings in a printed bracket fixed to the gripper body, and the pivot sits directly above the fingertip when the jaw is open about 42 mm. The gripper servo drives it through a 15 mm horn crank and a printed connecting rod (MR63 at both ends) to a 30 mm lever on the jaw, about a 2:1 reduction. The jaw turns only about 0.57 rad over a 10 to 100 mm opening, so the fingertip stays on a near-flat arc: under 11 mm of rise at 100 mm and about 6 mm at 92 mm. The face turns at most 19 deg. The existing TPU pads are re-mounted with pad_angle about 0, and squeeze stays about 20 N. The fingertip height is the same as the stock jaw's, so the start-pose clearance that sank the reach_mm trials does not change.
ideas.test:
The simulator needs a revolute jaw builder with a configurable pivot position (height above the tip and horizontal offset) and a servo-to-jaw ratio from a crank-rocker. That is the existing revolute model with R and the phase as parameters, plus a reduction on the jaw angle. Then re-run all 21 groups with System 1 refitting pad_angle_deg around 0 to 10.

Cost: 4 × $0.90 = $3.60, 3 days lead time, about 150 machine minutes for 30 g of PLA. That is within the $40 budget, 7 days and 595 minutes.

ideas.name: cam-compensated drop pad on the stock revolute jaw (inclined slide, two-slot cam keeps the tip level and the face vertical)
ideas.description: The stock hinged jaw is unchanged. A pad carriage on two 3 mm rods with LM3UU bushings rides a slide inclined 15 deg outward-down on the moving jaw. An MR63 follower on the carriage runs in a printed slot cam bolted to the gripper body, beside the hinge. The cam profile is flat for jaw angles up to about 0.4 rad, then drops the carriage by 81(1-cos(q-q0)) mm, which cancels the fingertip rise. A second MR63 follower on a pivoted TPU-skinned pad plate runs in a parallel slot, offset about 12 mm, and turns the face back by the jaw angle, keeping it vertical. For openings under about 38 mm (dice, marker, wood block, screwdriver) the cam is flat and the pad behaves exactly like today's 20-deg pad. For wide openings the tip stays at fixed-jaw height and the face stays antipodal, and the maximum opening grows to about 100 mm.
ideas.test: Simulator builder needed: a revolute jaw whose pad frame gets a jaw-angle-dependent offset and rotation. Use dz(q) = -81(1-cos(q-0.4)) for q > 0.4 (else 0), dx = dz*tan15deg outward, and face rotation -(q-0.36) for q > 0.36, all as a kinematic coupling to the gripper joint. Add 22 g at the moving jaw. Then re-run all 21 objects with System 1 re-tuning.

Contacts must be horizontal and opposed, and the fingertip must reach below the object's top. Higher friction (TPU 0.9) holds the leftover tilt, since squeeze-out needs N sin(a) > mu N

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face, with fixed_jaw_missed and force_limit on tuna as the same root cause. The hinged jaw's fingertip rises about R(1-cos q), with R = 81 mm, as it opens. From the brief: +11 mm at 65 mm, +18 mm at 75 mm and +28 mm at 85 mm. The objects that fail are wide and low: pudding is 90 mm wide with its top at +19 mm from centre, sugar 92 mm (top +23), mustard 96 mm (top +29) and tuna 85 mm (34 mm tall). The traces show the moving pad pushing down on the top face at 74 to 88 deg, at +18 to +28 mm, which is level with the top. Mustard at 96 mm is also past the widest opening of 91 mm.
proposals.principle: A finger can hold an object's side only if its tip reaches below the object's top at that object's opening. A finger that slides straight along the closing axis does not turn and does not rise, so its face stays antipodal to the fixed face and its tip stays at the fixed tip's height at every opening. Squeeze on a slide is servo torque divided by the effective pinion radius.
proposals.hypothesis: No catalogue part covers 17 to 96 mm with a low fingertip. Pads are the only cheap lever: past 20 deg they lowered the wide-opening tip, but at 30 deg they lost dice, foam_brick, large_marker, racquetball and wood_block, and at 45 deg they lost 12 groups. reach_mm and pad_tpu_mm do not change the rise. Parallelogram links rise more: +49 mm at 85 mm with 90 mm links. The prismatic jaw tops out at 58 mm, which would lose apple, banana, gelatin, tennis and tomato. 12 V servos are refused on budget and do not touch this mechanism anyway. The iteration-2 geared prismatic idea depended on 150 mm rods, which the manifest does not list. This version is buildable entirely from manifest items. Each 3x100 rod carries a single LM3UU (10 mm long) on a 12 mm carriage, which leaves 88 mm of stroke. A printed 2:1 step-up (40-tooth gear on the servo horn driving a 20-tooth gear on an idler shaft cut from a third 3x100 rod, in two MR63 bearings) turns a 46-tooth module-1 pinion (23 mm pitch radius). Travel is 23 mm x 2 x 1.92 rad = 88 mm, so with a 14 mm minimum gap the jaw opens from 14 to 102 mm, covering dice at 17 mm through mustard at 96 mm. Squeeze is 1.62/(0.023 x 2), about 35 N less gear friction, which is more than the current 20 N. Sugar at 514 g on friction 0.5 needs about 7.6 N with a 1.5x margin for the lift. Shoulder load is 0.41 + 0.15 x 5.14 = 1.18 N*m, plus about 0.1 N*m for the roughly 70 g module, still under the 1.62 N*m stall. The pads must go to pad_angle_deg=0 on a non-turning finger, otherwise the face sits at -20 deg. A small groove (about 2 mm) would centre the round held objects.
risks: Round held objects (golf_ball, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple, lemon, plum, strawberry, tomato_soup_can): two flat vertical faces do not trap a sphere on their own. A 2 mm groove and contact at the equator (the tip no longer rises, so System 1 can set the height) should keep them.

dice and large_marker: the narrow end of the stroke must close below 17 mm. The 14 mm minimum gap leaves 3 mm, and squeeze rises to about 35 N, so the force limit on light objects may need a softer close target from System 1.
potted_meat_can (370 g) and sugar: the extra wrist mass of about 70 g adds about 0.1 N*m at the shoulder, giving about 1.3 N*m against the 1.62 N*m stall.
foam_brick: 35 N on foam can trip the force limit, but System 1 controls the close target, and the slide's squeeze is the same at every opening, so it is predictable.

idea.name: stepped-up rack jaw on 100 mm rods
idea.description: A carriage slides on two 3x100 mm steel rods, one LM3UU bushing per rod, and holds the moving finger with its face vertical and parallel to the fixed jaw. A printed module-1 rack on the carriage is driven by a 46-tooth pinion on an idler shaft (a cut 3 mm rod in two MR63 bearings). A printed 40:20 spur pair from the servo horn steps the speed up 2:1, so the servo's 1.92 rad turns the pinion 3.84 rad: 88 mm of straight stroke, a 14 to 102 mm opening, and about 35 N of squeeze. The fingertip neither turns nor rises, so it reaches the side of a box 38 mm tall at 90 mm, where the hinge leaves it 28 to 31 mm high. Keep the existing TPU pads with pad_angle_deg=0, and add a groove of about 2 mm for spheres.
idea.test: A prismatic jaw whose finger travels 46 mm per servo radian (23 mm pinion pitch radius x 2:1 gear), with an 88 mm stroke (opening 14 to 102 mm) and squeeze = servo torque / 0.046 m less about 10% gear loss, plus about 70 g at the wrist. Pads at pad_angle_deg=0 with groove_mm of about 2. Run all 21 objects, especially pudding, sugar, mustard and tuna, and the round held ones (golf_ball, racquetball, apple, tennis_ball, lemon, plum, strawberry, tomato_soup_can) and dice at the narrow end.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: stepped-up rack jaw on 100 mm rods; it would need $8.70 from the manifest, 3 days, 200 machine min; within the budget left

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding_box, sugar_box, mustard_bottle), plus fixed_jaw_missed and force_limit at t=0.02 s on tuna_fish_can. These come from one geometric limit. The hinged moving jaw opens 91 mm at most, but these objects are 85 to 96 mm across. Near that width the moving fingertip has risen +28 mm at 85 mm, and about +33 mm at 90 mm by interpolation, while the face is 42 deg off parallel. The jaw therefore lands on the object's top. The traces show this: pudding contact at +18 mm with the top at +19, pushing 86 deg down; sugar at +21 with the top at +23; mustard at +28 with the top at +29.
proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by about R(1 - cos q). A finger can only hold a side if, at that opening, its tip reaches below the object's top. If the swing is centred on the bottom of the arc, not started there, the rise is split into a small dip mid-range and a small rise at the ends. A parallelogram keeps the face vertical at every opening, so the contact stays antipodal.
proposals.hypothesis: Nothing in the catalogue can fix this. The revolute jaw tops out at 91 mm with +28 mm of tip rise. Pads at 30 or 45 deg trade wide-object tilt for small-object losses (iteration 1 lost 5 to 12 groups and never gained pudding or tuna). The prismatic jaw tops out at 58 mm. The catalogue parallelogram starts its links hanging straight down, so the tip only rises: +49 mm at 85 mm with link 90. The 12 V servos are refused on budget and add torque, not travel. The arm has torque to spare even for sugar_box: 0.41 + 0.15 x 5.14 = 1.18 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall. The proposal is the catalogue parallelogram four-bar with 95 mm links, mounted with the servo horn offset so the links lean about 0.42 rad toward closing when the jaw is shut. The servo then sweeps about -0.42 to +0.58 rad, inside its -0.17..1.55 rad range once offset. Horizontal travel is 95 x (sin 0.42 + sin 0.58) ≈ 92 mm, giving an opening from about 8 mm to about 100 mm, enough to clear the 96 mm mustard bottle. The tip height relative to the closed tip is 95 x (cos 0.42 - cos θ): it dips about 8 mm mid-range at around 50 mm openings and rises only about +7 mm at the widest opening. At pudding's 90 mm the tip sits at about +4 mm against a 38 mm tall box, and at tuna's 85 mm at about +1 mm against 34 mm. The face does not turn, so the pad's built-in tilt must go to 0 deg on this jaw. Squeeze is torque over lever: 1.62 / (0.095 cos θ) ≈ 17 to 21 N, the same as the current 20 N. This is a different idea from the two rack designs recorded earlier. It needs no rods, only four bearings and one printed part, and it keeps the stock jaw's compact hinge motion. The stepped-up rack jaw from iteration 3 is still the fallback if the mid-range dip turns out to touch the table.
risks: dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube: at the closed end the face is parallel and the tip is level with the fixed one, the same as now (the revolute jaw now has the face 12 deg off and the tip at -0 mm at 17 mm), so they should hold. The links do lean, though, and the actual minimum gap needs checking.

golf_ball, strawberry, plum, foam_brick, racquetball, cup, potted_meat_can, lemon (42 to 59 mm): this is where the tip dips, up to about 8 mm below the fixed fingertip. If the fixed tip clears the table by less than that, the moving tip strikes the table. In the simulator, the grasp height or the phase offset (0.30 to 0.42 rad) must be checked so the dip stays above the table. Round objects are gripped slightly below the equator, which pushes them up, and TPU friction of 0.9 must hold that.

apple, banana, tennis_ball, tomato_soup_can, gelatin_box (66 to 75 mm): the face is parallel here, where today it is 23 to 32 deg off, and the tip is near level, so these should improve rather than break.
All groups: two 95 mm printed links and four bearings add roughly 20 g at the wrist. That is small against the 0.44 N*m of shoulder margin even with the 514 g sugar box.

idea.name: phase-offset parallelogram jaw (links leaning toward closing at the closed position)
idea.description: A four-bar parallelogram carries the moving finger without turning it, as the catalogue part does. The difference is that the servo horn and both links are indexed so the links lean about 0.42 rad toward the fixed jaw when the jaw is closed. As the servo opens the jaw, the finger's arc of radius 95 mm passes through its lowest point near the middle of the range rather than starting there. The tip height then varies by only about -8/+7 mm over the whole 8 to 100 mm opening, where the stock hinge rises +28 mm by 85 mm. Because the face stays vertical, both contacts stay horizontal and opposed, and the moving pad is printed at 0 deg tilt. The servo sweep is about 1.0 rad, and squeeze is 17 to 21 N.
idea.test: Add a phase_rad parameter (range 0 to 0.6 rad, the link lean at the closed position) to the parallelogram jaw builder. The servo zero is indexed by that offset, and the opening and tip height come from 95 cos(θ) and 95 sin(θ) across the sweep from -phase_rad to the servo limit. Run it with link_mm=95, phase_rad=0.42 and the pad's tilt at 0 deg. Check the table-clearance dip for the 42 to 59 mm objects first.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: phase-offset parallelogram jaw (links leaning toward closing at the closed position); it would need $3.60 from the manifest, 3 days, 118 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes:
The four failing objects (pudding_box, sugar_box, mustard_bottle, tuna_fish_can) can't be fixed with the catalogue parts within budget, so this batch is one idea and nothing that runs in a trial.

**Why nothing in the catalogue works:**
- **Hinged jaw (current):** it opens 91 mm at most, which is narrower than sugar_box (92 mm) and mustard_bottle (96 mm). Even at 85 mm the moving fingertip has risen 28 mm and its face is 42 deg off parallel, so it lands on the object's top. Pads can tilt the face but don't lower the fingertip enough, and the pad changes in iteration 1 lost 5 to 12 held groups.
- **Prismatic jaw:** it opens 58 mm at most.
- **Catalogue parallelogram jaw:** its fingertip rises more than the current jaw's, 49 mm at 85 mm.
- **12 V servos:** refused at $68 against the $40 left, and they add lifting torque, not opening width. The arm has enough torque anyway: holding the 514 g sugar box takes 1.18 N*m against a 1.62 N*m stall.

**The idea:** the same parallelogram jaw with its links leaning toward the fixed jaw when shut. The fingertip's arc then has its lowest point mid-range instead of at the start. That gives an opening from about 8 to 100 mm, with the fingertip within about -8/+7 mm of its closed height and the face always vertical. Grip force stays at 17 to 21 N.

**Cost:** $3.60 for four bearings, 3 days lead time, and about 120 printer minutes; everything else is on hand.

**Main risk:** the 8 mm dip happens at 42 to 59 mm openings, where eight held objects sit. The fingertip could hit the table there, so the simulator check should test that first.

**Fallback:** the stepped-up rack jaw on 100 mm rods (idea from iteration 3, $8.70, all parts on the manifest) has the same aim. It would be the choice if the dip can't be kept above the table.

**No trials this round:** the record shows that every way of changing the pads either breaks small-object groups or fails to gain the wide ones. Another pad trial would just risk held groups again.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding_box, sugar_box, mustard_bottle; tuna_fish_can's fixed_jaw_missed and force_limit come from the same geometry). The hinged moving fingertip swings on an 81 mm radius, so it rises by about R(1 - cos q). The brief gives +18 mm at 75 mm, +28 mm at 85 mm, and the widest opening is 91 mm. The failing objects need 85 to 96 mm and their tops sit only +17 (tuna), +19 (pudding), +23 (sugar) and +29 mm (mustard) above the grasp centre. In the trials the moving pad landed on the top face at +18 to +28 mm, pushing 74 to 88 deg down.
proposals.principle: A finger can hold an object's side only if, at that object's opening, the fingertip reaches below the object's top. A finger that slides straight along the closing axis neither turns nor rises, so its face stays parallel and its tip stays level at every opening.
proposals.hypothesis: No `params` move works. Pads only re-aim the face. The rise per degree of pad angle is about 0.56 mm, so even 45 deg leaves +14 mm at 85 mm, and iteration 1 showed that 30 to 45 deg loses 5 to 12 held groups without gaining a wide box. reach_mm extends both pads, so the relative rise stays the same or grows by r(1 - cos q). No catalogue swap works either. The parallelogram rises more (+49 mm at 85 mm with 90 mm links). The prismatic jaw tops out at 58 mm and would lose apple, banana, gelatin, tennis and tomato. servos_12v is refused at $68 against $40 and targets arm torque, which is not the failure: sugar needs about 1.18 N*m of 1.62. Prismatic ideas recorded earlier needed gear stages or 150 mm rods. This idea keeps the stock hinge and servo and changes only how the finger is constrained. The moving pad sits on a printed carriage that slides in a printed horizontal dovetail track on the gripper body, at fingertip height. The stock jaw lever becomes a slotted lever: a bearing-rollered pin on the carriage rides in a slot cut along the lever. The carriage then moves x = h*tan(q) with h = 81 mm. Tip rise is 0 at every opening, and the face is parallel at every opening if pad_angle is set to 0. Travel from q = -0.17 to 0.82 rad is about 14 + 86 = 100 mm, enough for mustard's 96 mm within the servo's -0.17 to 1.20 rad. Squeeze is about tau*cos^2(q)/h: 20 N near closed (as now for dice and marker) and about 9.5 N at 96 mm. Friction needs about 6 N for the 514 g sugar box and about 6.3 N for the 431 g mustard bottle at mu 0.4 to 0.5 with a 1.2 margin, so 9.5 N is enough. It adds about 35 g of PLA at the wrist, about 0.05 N*m at the shoulder, which leaves margin under 1.62 N*m.
risks: dice and large_marker currently pass with the face 12 deg off, bottom swung in. A parallel face loses that inward bias, but TPU at friction 0.9 and 20 N near closed should still hold them.

Rolling objects (golf_ball, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple, lemon, plum, strawberry, tomato_soup_can) are held at the equator. Zero rise puts both contacts at the same height, which should help. Squeeze at 66 to 75 mm falls to about 12 to 14 N, still several times the 0.6 to 3.4 N their weights need.
potted_meat_can (370 g, friction 0.35, 57 mm) gets about 17 N at its opening against roughly 6.2 N needed.
foam_brick hit force_limit at higher squeeze in iteration 1. The yoke's squeeze at 52 mm (about 17 N) is below today's 20 N.

idea.name: slotted-lever (Scotch-yoke) straight-line jaw
idea.description: The stock jaw servo turns a printed slotted lever about the existing hinge axis. A pin on the moving-pad carriage, fitted with an MR63 bearing as a roller, rides in the lever's slot. The carriage slides in a printed dovetail track fixed to the gripper body, running along the closing axis at fingertip height (h = 81 mm below the hinge axis). The carriage only translates, x = h*tan(q), so the moving face stays parallel to the fixed face and the moving tip stays level with the fixed tip at every opening from 0 to about 100 mm. Squeeze is servo torque*cos^2(q)/h, which is 20 N near closed and about 9.5 N fully open. A second MR63 on the carriage's track side cuts sliding friction. The pads keep a TPU skin with pad_angle 0. Unlike the recorded geared and rack ideas, it needs no rods, no gear stage and no new purchases beyond two bearings.
idea.test: A jaw type 'slotted_yoke' with parameter h_mm in [60, 100]. The moving finger is a prismatic joint along the closing axis, coupled to the servo angle by x = h*tan(q - q0) (equality/tendon coupling, or a pin-in-slot contact pair), with the face kept at 0 deg and the tip at the fixed tip's height. Squeeze is limited to servo torque*cos^2(q)/h. Wrist mass is about 35 g extra.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face, which covers all 4 failing groups (pudding 90 mm, sugar 92 mm, mustard 96 mm, tuna 85 mm; tuna's fixed_jaw_missed and force_limit come from the same high, over-opened moving tip). The moving fingertip swings on a circle of R = 81 mm. Its lowest point sits near a 25 mm opening (q ≈ 0.24 rad: brief tip -0 mm at 17/25 mm, +1 mm at 35 mm). Wide objects are therefore gripped far up the arc: +18 mm at 75 mm, +28 mm at 85 mm, and 90-96 mm is past the widest opening of 91 mm. The trials put the moving pad at +18..+28 mm, right at the top faces (+17..+29 mm), pushing 74-88 deg down.
proposals.principle: The fingertip rises by about R(1 - cos q) from the bottom of its arc, which is roughly s²/2R for a sideways offset s from that bottom. Rise grows with the square of the offset, so the fix is to centre the needed opening range (17-96 mm) on the bottom of the arc. Right now everything sits on one side of it. Moving the fixed face outward by d moves the arc's lowest point to an opening of 25 + d mm without changing the servo, the hinge or the 81 mm radius. A face that pivots freely seats flat on a flat side, so the contact normal stays horizontal however far the jaw has swung. That removes the face-tilt cost of using a wider arc.
proposals.hypothesis:
Use d = 20 mm, putting the lowest point at a 45 mm opening. Rise is 81(1 - cos(asin(s/81))) with s = width - 45.
- Wide objects: tuna 85 mm gives s = 40, rise 10.6 mm (top +17). Pudding 90 gives 13.6 mm (top +19). Sugar 92 gives 15 mm (top +22.5). Mustard 96 gives 18 mm (top +29). All four contacts land below the top with 4-11 mm to spare, compared with 0-1 mm of overlap now.
- Small objects: dice 17 mm gives s = -28, rise 5 mm (top +8.5). The marker gets 4.3 mm (top +9.5) and the wood cube 2.3 mm (top +13).
- Servo range: dice needs q ≈ -0.11 rad and mustard q ≈ 0.92 rad, both inside the -0.17..1.20 range. At -0.17 rad the jaw closes to about 12.7 mm, leaving 4 mm of squeeze travel on the dice. At 1.20 rad it opens to about 113 mm, so 96 mm objects fit with side clearance.
- Why the pivot pad is needed: the jaw angle used grows to about 1.0 rad, so a rigid pad would see about -20 deg (dice) to +39 deg (mustard). Iteration 1 showed that about -22 deg loses dice, marker and wood block, and tan 39° = 0.81 exceeds cardboard's μ of 0.5. The pad pivots on an M3 pin in two MR63 bearings, limited to ±40 deg by printed stops, with a light centring spring. It seats flush on boxes, cans and dice.
- Grip and arm load: squeeze stays about 20 N (same lever). 2μN = 20 N, against 5.0 N for the sugar box and 4.2 N for the mustard. The shoulder needs 0.41 + 0.15 × 5.14 = 1.18 N·m, under the 1.62 N·m stall.
- Why cheaper moves fail: no pad parameter moves the arc's lowest point. reach_mm extends both pads, which adds R(1 - cos) to the relative rise. pad_angle trades rise for small-object tilt; iteration 1 lost 5-12 groups at 30-45 deg and gained no wide box. The prismatic jaw tops out at 58 mm (loses apple, banana, gelatin, tennis, tomato). Parallelogram links rise +49 mm at 85 mm. The 12 V servos are refused ($68 > $40) and torque is not the mechanism. This idea differs from the four ideas already recorded, which were all new straight-line drives. It keeps the stock hinge and servo and only moves the fixed face and frees the moving face.
risks: dice / large_marker: the moving contact sits 4-5 mm higher than now (half-heights 8.5 and 9.5 mm), and the jaw closes near the servo floor (about 4 mm of travel left). Should hold because the pivot pad keeps the face vertical, which avoids iteration 1's squeezed_up_out failure.

rolling objects (golf, lemon, plum, racquetball, strawberry, apple, tennis, tomato can): with a free pad, the force acts along the line from the pivot to the ball's centre, not along a fixed face normal. The centring spring and ±40 deg stops bound this. Rise drops for 53-96 mm objects (apple at 75 mm: about 6 mm instead of 18), which should help them.
all groups: the grasp centre moves about 10 mm toward the fixed jaw. System 1 re-tunes grasp.side to absorb it.
gelatin_box: rise at 73 mm drops from about 17 mm to 5.4 mm against a 15 mm top, so it should improve.

idea.name: offset fixed finger with a self-aligning pivot pad on the moving jaw
idea.description: 1) A reprinted fixed jaw (gripper base) whose vertical face sits 20 mm farther from the moving jaw, at the same height. The stock fixed jaw is part of the gripper body, so the base is reprinted rather than given a bolt-on spacer, which would leave the old face in the way. The gripper servo and hinge are reused unchanged. The arc's lowest point moves from a 25 mm to a 45 mm opening. From 17 to 96 mm the fingertip then stays within 5-18 mm of the fixed tip, compared with up to +28 mm at 85 mm now (and 90-96 mm out of reach). 2) The moving pad is replaced by a TPU-skinned pad on an M3 pivot pin running in two MR63 bearings, with printed stops at ±40 deg and a light return spring. It seats flush on flat sides at any jaw angle, so the contact normal stays horizontal and antipodal to the fixed face. The fixed pad stays as it is now (TPU, 12 mm wide).

needs.item: small torsion/return spring (or printed TPU flexure)

idea.test: Simulator needs: (a) a fixed-jaw x-offset parameter (0-30 mm) that moves the fixed face and its pad horizontally; (b) a moving pad with a hinge joint on its jaw (pivot about 3 mm behind the face at mid-pad, range ±40 deg, small spring stiffness and damping). proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding, sugar, mustard) and fixed_jaw_missed / force_limit (tuna). At 85-96 mm the hinged jaw has to swing so far that its fingertip rises 13-18 mm above the fixed one and lands on the top face (86 deg pushing down). The face is also 32-42 deg off parallel.
proposals.principle: A fingertip on a swinging joint rises by R(1-cos q). At a set opening, the swing is Δ = R sin q, so the rise is R - sqrt(R² - Δ²) ≈ Δ²/2R. A longer radius needs a smaller angle for the same opening, so the tip rises less and the face tilts less. The brief fits this model: with R = 81 and the faces parallel at about 25 mm, Δ = 60 gives a 27 mm rise, and the brief quotes +28 mm at 85 mm. The face tilt tracks the jaw angle q minus about 6 deg (17 mm: -12; 85 mm: +42).
proposals.hypothesis: reach_mm lengthens both pads past the stock fingertips, which raises the effective radius from about 81 to about 111 mm. Iteration 5 argued that the relative rise stays the same, but that holds only at a fixed servo angle; what matters is the rise at a given object width. Predicted with R = 111: at 85 mm the rise drops from 27 to 18 mm and the tilt from +42 to about +27 deg. At 90 mm: 33 to 21 mm and about +30 deg. At 92 mm: 35 to 22.5 mm. At 96 mm: about 26 mm, and the widest opening grows from 91 to about 115 mm, so the mustard bottle fits at all. About +30 deg is the tilt gelatin_box (73 mm, 30 deg today) already holds at with TPU, so pudding (0.5 friction, the same cardboard) should behave like gelatin. The failure logs show the hand puts the fixed contact near the object's centre height (pudding +0, sugar +7). If the longer pad also moves the tips lower against the object, pudding (top +19) and tuna (top +17) come under their tops. Sugar (+22.5) is marginal, and mustard (+29 top, 26 mm rise) is possible but not predicted. No `params` value of pad_angle helps: it moves the tip only about 0.56 mm per deg and cost 5-12 groups in iteration 1. Every catalogue swap is worse: the prismatic jaw tops out at 58 mm, the parallelogram rises +49 mm, and the 12 V servos cost $68 against $40 left. This is the only catalogue lever left untested at a large value. Iteration 1 tried reach only at 2-3 mm, and always mixed with pad angles of 30-45 deg. Cost: about 6 g extra PLA plus 1 g TPU, roughly 40 machine min, $0, everything on hand.

dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube (17-26 mm): small openings barely move the jaw, so their tilt changes little (dice -12 to about -10 deg). The risk is that a pad tip 30 mm longer reaches the table, if the controller does not account for the reach.

apple, tennis_ball, racquetball, lemon, plum, strawberry, golf_ball (round): if the contacts move below the equator they push the ball up. Their tilts actually fall (e.g. 66 mm: +23 to about +15 deg), which should help.

iterations.notes:
I'm proposing two parameter moves on the existing pads: lengthen both pads to reach_mm=30 or 16, and keep every other value. Both are untested, cost $0 (parts and filament on hand), and need about 20–40 machine minutes. Both change the same slot, so they will be tried separately, not together.

**Why lengthening the pads should help.** All four failing objects are 85–96 mm wide, near or past the jaw's widest opening. At that width the moving fingertip rises above the top face and lands on top of the object. Iterations 3–6 only recorded untested ideas, so this tests the one catalogue setting that hasn't been tried at a large value. Iteration 5 dismissed it on the grounds that the tip rise wouldn't change. That reasoning was wrong:
- At a given servo angle, a longer finger rises more. But what matters is the rise at a given object width, and that rise is roughly (opening swing)² / (2 × radius).
- A longer pad raises the radius from 81 mm to about 111 mm. At 90 mm the rise drops from about 33 mm to about 21 mm, and the moving face tilts about 30° instead of about 40°.
- The gelatin box already holds at about 30° tilt with the rubber (TPU) skin, so 30° should be holdable.
- The widest opening grows from 91 mm to about 115 mm, so the 96 mm mustard bottle fits for the first time.

**Expected gains.**
- reach_mm=30: pudding box and tuna can likely. Sugar box is borderline: its predicted rise of about 22.5 mm equals its 22.5 mm top. Mustard bottle is possible but not predicted.
- reach_mm=16: tuna can and pudding box only, and less surely; it is the safer hedge.

**Held groups at risk.**
- **Heavy cans (potted meat, tomato soup):** squeeze drops from about 20 N to about 15 N, which still leaves about 3× margin over their weight.
- **Short objects (dice, marker, wood cube):** a 30 mm longer fixed pad could hit the table. This depends on how the controller sets grasp height, which I can't tell from the logs.
- **Round objects:** if the contacts move below the middle of the ball they push it upward. Their face tilt drops, which should help.

**If neither change passes,** no catalogue part can fix this:
- the slide jaw opens only 58 mm;
- the four-bar jaw's fingertip rises even more (+49 mm at 85 mm);
- the 12 V servos cost $68 against the $40 left.

The next step would then be to build the cheapest recorded idea, the straight-line slotted-lever jaw ($1.80, 3 days, 183 machine minutes), rather than record another one.

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face (pudding, sugar, mustard) and fixed_jaw_missed/force_limit (tuna) both come from the same cause. The revolute jaw opens to only 91 mm, and its fingertip rises by about R(1 - cos q) on the 81 mm hinge: +18 mm at 75 mm, +28 mm at 85 mm, more at 90. Tuna (85 mm, top +17), pudding (90 mm, top +19), sugar (92 mm, top +23) and mustard (96 mm, top +29) are all wider than the opening or need a fingertip lower than the jaw can bring it. The traces show it: the moving pad lands on the top edge at +18 to +28 mm, pushing 74 to 88 deg down.
proposals.principle: A finger that slides in a straight line along the closing axis neither turns nor rises as it opens, so its face stays parallel and its tip stays below the top at every width. The opening is pitch radius × usable servo angle. The STS3215 is a 4096-step-per-turn position servo, so the gripper does not have to stay inside the 1.92 rad the catalogue prismatic assumes.
proposals.hypothesis: Nothing in the catalogue can do this. Revolute: the brief gives +28 mm of rise and 42 deg of tilt at 85 mm, and 91 mm maximum. Pads only re-aim the face: 30 to 45 deg lost 5 to 12 groups in iteration 1, and reach 16 to 30 lost 2 to 7 groups with no gain in iteration 7. Parallelogram link 90: +49 mm at 85 mm, worse. Prismatic: no rise (+2 mm), but at most 58 mm even at 60 teeth, because it is held to -0.17..1.75 rad. 12 V servos: refused ($68 > $40), and they do not touch this mechanism anyway. The fix is the prismatic module with the gripper servo's software angle limits widened to about 3.6 rad (about 205 deg; the servo's position range is 360 deg), driving a 48-tooth module-1 pinion (24 mm per rad). That gives about 84 mm of carriage travel, an opening of about 14 to 98 mm, a fingertip that stays level at every width, and a squeeze of 1.62/0.024 ≈ 67 N at stall (System 1 limits it through the close target). This fits on 100 mm rods: one LM3UU per rod on the carriage, so 100 - 10 (carriage) - 6 (clamps) = 84 mm. With pad_angle_deg reset to 0 the faces are parallel at every width. This is different from the iteration-2/3 geared ideas: there is no extra gear stage and no new item, only the servo's own range.
risks: foam_brick: it was lost before to force_limit, and the squeeze ceiling rises from 20 N to about 67 N. It survives if System 1 sets the close target just past contact.
potted_meat_can, tomato_soup_can (heavy, friction 0.35): racking of a short single-bushing carriage under 35 to 37 N of weight torque. The rod spacing must be at least 25 mm.
dice, large_marker (17 to 19 mm): needs a minimum opening of 14 mm or less. Kept by setting the rack end stop at 14 mm.

Rolling objects (golf_ball, plum, lemon, racquetball, tennis_ball, apple): flat parallel faces with no groove. The current flat pads already hold them, and with no tilt there is no squeeze-out at any width.
mustard_bottle itself is marginal: 98 mm of opening against 96 mm leaves about 1 mm per side.

idea.name: full-turn rack jaw (prismatic jaw with the gripper servo's position range widened to about 205 deg)
idea.description: A printed 48-tooth module-1 pinion (50 mm across) on the gripper servo horn drives a printed rack on a carriage. The carriage rides two 3 x 100 mm steel rods on one LM3UU bushing per rod. The fixed finger sits on the frame just past the far end of the rods. The STS3215 angle limits (min/max angle registers) are widened from about 110 deg to about 205 deg of its 360-deg, 4096-step range. Travel is 24 mm per rad × 3.5 rad ≈ 84 mm, so the opening runs from about 14 to 98 mm. The finger neither turns nor rises (the catalogue prismatic shows +2 mm at every width), so the pad stays parallel to the fixed face and reaches below the top of the 34 to 58 mm-tall wide objects. The TPU pads are kept with pad_angle_deg=0. Squeeze is servo torque over the 24 mm pitch radius: up to about 67 N, set lower by the close target. Sugar at 514 g needs only 2·0.5·N > 7.6 N.
idea.test: Use the existing prismatic jaw builder with two changes: pinion_teeth=48 (beyond its current 17-60 sampling is fine), and the gripper joint range raised from -0.17..1.75 to -0.17..3.6 rad, with carriage travel capped at 84 mm by the 100 mm rods. Set pads to pad_angle_deg=0, pad_tpu_mm=2. Run all 21 objects, and check the 17 mm dice/marker at the low end and the 96 mm mustard at the top.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: full-turn rack jaw (prismatic jaw with the gripper servo's position range widened to about 205 deg); it would need $5.40 from the manifest, 3 days, 158 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes:
I'm sending one proposal, an idea, because no params move or catalogue swap can fix the remaining four groups.

- **Sugar (92 mm) and mustard (96 mm):** both are wider than the revolute jaw's 91 mm maximum opening.
- **Tuna (85 mm) and pudding (90 mm):** the moving fingertip sits +28 to +33 mm above the fixed one at those widths, but the tops are only +17 and +19 mm above it.

The record has already ruled out every cheap lever:
- Pads with a 30 to 45 deg angle lost 5 to 12 held groups.
- Pads with 16 to 30 mm of reach lost 2 to 7 held groups and gained nothing.
- The parallelogram jaw's fingertip rises more, not less: +49 mm at 85 mm.
- The catalogue prismatic jaw stops at 58 mm.
- 12 V servos would cost $68 against $40 left, and they don't address this failure anyway.

The idea differs from the earlier geared-rack ideas because it adds no gear stage and no item the manifest lacks. It widens the gripper servo's software angle limits (the STS3215 can turn a full 360 deg) and drives a larger pinion on the catalogue's 100 mm rods. That gives about 84 mm of travel, an opening of about 14 to 98 mm, and a fingertip that stays level as the jaw opens. It costs $5.40 (2 LM3UU bushings, 2 rods), takes 3 days and about 158 machine minutes, all within budget.

To test it, the existing prismatic builder needs only a wider joint range. I would run that first to check the mustard (marginal at about 1 mm per side) and the foam brick (higher squeeze) before printing anything.

proposals.edit: pads (groove_mm=0, lip_mm=0, pad_angle_deg=20, pad_tpu_mm=0.5, reach_mm=0, width_mm=12)
proposals.mechanism: fixed_jaw_missed and force_limit on tuna_fish_can, and moving_jaw_on_top_face on the 90 mm boxes. All of these come from running the hinged jaw at the end of its range. The stock jaw opens 91 mm at most, and at 85 mm it needs servo 1.08 rad, which gives +28 mm of tip rise and 42 deg of tilt. Tuna (85 mm) leaves about 3 mm of clearance per side, and rva000_tuna hits the force limit at t=0.02 s, i.e. on the can during descent.
proposals.principle: Face separation equals jaw separation minus twice the pad thickness. Thinner pads reach a given object width at a smaller servo angle. Tip rise R(1-cos q) grows roughly with the square of q at the wide end, and tilt grows with q, so a smaller angle at the same width means less rise, less tilt and more room. From the brief's table, the jaw follows width ≈ 22.6 + 81 sin(q-0.20) and rise ≈ 81(1-cos(q-0.20)) (it reproduces the 17/55/85 mm rows). Taking 1.5 mm off each face moves the curve 3 mm wider. Tuna then needs q ≈ 1.02 instead of 1.08: rise about 26 mm instead of about 29, tilt about 39 deg instead of 42. The widest opening grows to about 94 mm, so the clearance at 85 mm goes from about 3 to about 4.5 mm per side.
proposals.hypothesis: pad_tpu_mm has never been varied on its own. Every past pad trial moved pad_angle or reach, which re-aim or lengthen the face. This one moves only the face's offset. The brief says any TPU skin gives friction 0.9, so a 0.5 mm skin should keep the friction the cans and gelatin rely on while thinning each face from 5 to about 3.5 mm. It is the cheapest move left that changes the angle the jaw needs for a given width. I don't expect it to fix pudding, sugar or mustard: at 90 mm the face would still be about 45 deg off parallel, and mustard (96 mm) stays out of reach. It is mainly a shot at tuna, which fails on clearance and placement rather than on rise alone.
risks: large_marker, dice, wood_block_cube: small objects now need about 0.03-0.04 rad less servo, so the moving face swings about 2-3 deg further bottom-in (12 to about 14-15 deg at 17 mm). Iteration 1 lost large_marker at about 22 deg (squeezed_up_out). 15 deg is well inside the TPU friction cone (tan 15 = 0.27 < 0.9), so they should hold.

gelatin_box, apple, tomato_soup_can, tennis_ball: their servo angle also drops, which lowers both tilt and rise, so this should help them. The one risk is if the simulator scales TPU friction with skin thickness instead of the brief's flat 0.9, which would hit gelatin first.
proposals.result: rejected: gained nothing; still failing: force_limit, moving_jaw_on_top_face

proposals.mechanism: moving_jaw_on_top_face on pudding_box, sugar_box and mustard_bottle (contacts 74-88 deg pushing down, at the object's top). It has two causes that no catalogue part removes together. (1) The face turns with its joint: revolute 42 deg at 85 mm, and pads only shift where it is parallel; at 30-45 deg they lost 5-12 held groups. (2) The fingertip rises: revolute +28 mm at 85 mm; parallelogram (link 90) keeps the face square but rises +49 mm at 85 mm; prismatic tops out at 58 mm.
proposals.principle: A finger holds a side only if its face is vertical (antipodal to the fixed face) and its tip reaches below the object's top. The parallelogram fixes the orientation at every opening. A gravity drop-slide on the finger lets the tip find the table whatever the carriage rise. The horizontal squeeze passes through a friction-lined guide, so once the jaw clamps, the slide locks (μN = 0.9 × 20-37 N = 18-33 N against at most 5 N of object weight). With no squeeze, the slide runs free.
proposals.hypothesis: This combination has not been recorded. The earlier ideas fought the rise kinematically (offset circles, racks, yokes). This one makes the rise irrelevant: the finger always stands on the table with a vertical face, at every width from 17 to about 96 mm. With link_mm 90 and pad_angle 0, the parallelogram already reaches 96 mm, and moving the finger face 3-4 mm outboard on the carriage covers mustard. It needs the $3.60 of bearings the catalogue parallelogram already calls for, and nothing else is bought.
risks: Tall objects (potted_meat_can, cup): when the jaw is nearly closed, the slide must retract up to about 60 mm above the carriage. The finger has to telescope, or it will hit the wrist housing.
Sugar box at 514 g adds the finger's ~12 g at the wrist: shoulder about 0.41 + 0.79 = 1.20 N*m, still under the 1.62 N*m stall.

idea.name: squeeze-locked drop finger on a parallelogram jaw
idea.description: Start from the catalogue parallelogram jaw (link_mm 90, pad_angle_deg 0) so the moving face stays vertical at every opening. On its carriage, the finger is no longer rigid: it rides a vertical slot on two M3 screw pins (about 60 mm of travel, telescoping in two stages). With no load, the finger drops under its own weight until a low-friction PLA foot rests on the table, so the tip stays at table level however much the carriage rises (+49 mm at 85 mm). The slot's load-bearing wall is lined with TPU. Once the jaw clamps, the 20-37 N squeeze presses the pins against the lining and locks the slide by friction, so on lift the finger rises with the carriage. The face is TPU-skinned (0.9). The finger face sits 3-4 mm outboard so the opening reaches about 100 mm.
idea.test: In the simulator, give the parallelogram finger a child body on a vertical slide joint (0 to 60 mm, gravity-driven), with a foot geom that collides with the table. Model the squeeze lock as slide friction proportional to the jaw's normal load (or a contact pair between the pin and a TPU-friction slot wall). Then run all 21 objects, checking the 17-19 mm small objects and the 84 mm potted_meat_can for collisions between the retracted finger and the wrist.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: squeeze-locked drop finger on a parallelogram jaw; it would need $3.60 from the manifest, 3 days, 146 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes:
I checked every catalogue part against the brief's numbers, and none of them makes the moving face vertical and puts its tip below the object's top at 85-96 mm at the same time. Revolute gives +28 mm / 42 deg at 85 mm and opens 91 mm at most. Parallelogram (link 90) rises +49 mm at 85 mm. Prismatic tops out at 58 mm. servos_12v is refused on budget and doesn't address the mechanism anyway. The iteration 1 and 7 pad trials already cover pad_angle and reach.

So proposal 1 is the one untried, cheap knob: a thinner TPU skin, which moves the face rather than turning it, and I'm claiming only tuna for it. Proposal 2 is a new idea, not a repeat. Instead of fighting the tip rise with kinematics like the earlier ideas, it adds a gravity drop-slide to the parallelogram's square-held finger, locked by the squeeze.

Purchase if proposal 2 is ever built: 4 × mr63_bearing at $0.90 = $3.60, 3 days lead time. Machine time is about 146 minutes, within the 595 left.

Only one jaw swings, so at wide openings its fingertip sits well above the fixed one and its face is tilted bottom-out. It reaches the side of a short, wide object only at the top corner and presses on the top face. Numbers from the brief: tip +18 mm at 75 mm, +28 mm at 85 mm, and about +33 mm at the 90 mm pudding width; moving face 32 to 42 deg off parallel; widest opening 91 mm, below sugar (92) and mustard (96). proposals.principle: The rise is R(1 - cos q) for the one jaw that turns through the whole angle q. If both jaws hinge and are geared to swing equally and oppositely, each turns only about q/2. Both tips then rise by the same small amount, so the relative rise is zero, and each face tilts only half as much and symmetrically. With a 2:1 reduction from the servo to each jaw, the squeeze stays T/R ≈ 20 N, because the virtual work is T dq = 2·N·R·d(q/2). The full opening then comes from two half-swings, so it can go past 96 mm.
proposals.hypothesis: The catalogue cannot fix this, and the record proves it. Six pads-only trials gained 0 groups: angle 25/28/30/45, reach 8/16/30, and TPU 0.5 mm, which opened about 94 mm and still did not get the 90 mm pudding. So the opening alone is not enough; the rise and the tilt have to go too. Prismatic tops out at 58 mm and would lose apple, banana, gelatin, tennis and the tomato can. Parallelogram link 90 rises +49 mm at 85 mm, worse than now. 12 V servos are refused on budget ($68 vs $40) and do not address the geometry anyway. All six ideas recorded so far keep a rigid fixed jaw and try to straighten the moving one. This idea is different: it makes the closing symmetric. The stock fixed jaw is replaced by a mirror hinged jaw that a printed gear pair couples to the servo. Each jaw moves roughly ±20 deg about a parallel point near a 55 to 60 mm opening, set with pad_angle. Expected effect: both tips stay within about 81(1-cos20) ≈ 5 mm of each other's height and of the closed height at every width from 17 to about 105 mm, so the arm can lower both pads to table clearance beside a 34 to 58 mm tall box. Each face tilts at most about 13 to 17 deg across the whole range, compared with 42 deg now. Squeeze stays about 20 N, so the friction margins of the heavy objects held now are unchanged: potted meat 370 g, tomato soup can 349 g, and sugar 514 g with 2·0.5·20 = 20 N against 5 N of weight. The start-pose force_limit on tuna also goes away, because the 85 mm can no longer sits at the edge of a 91 mm opening.

potted_meat_can / tomato_soup_can: the squeeze stays about 20 N only if the gear ratio is 2:1. A 1:1 coupling would halve it to about 10 N and thin the margin on the 370 g can (2·0.35·10 = 7 N against 3.6 N of weight).

idea.name: geared symmetric twin-hinge jaw (both jaws swing, 2:1 reduction to each)
idea.description: The stock fixed jaw is replaced by a printed hinged jaw that mirrors the moving one, pivoting on two MR63 bearings in a printed bracket on the gripper body. The stock moving jaw gets a matching pair of MR63 bearings and a printed gear rim. A printed spur gear on the gripper servo horn drives both jaw gears in opposite directions at 2:1, so each jaw turns half the servo angle. The existing TPU pads (pad_tpu 2 mm, friction 0.9) go on both jaws. pad_angle sets where both faces are parallel, aimed at about a 55 to 60 mm opening, so the faces tilt symmetrically within about ±15 deg across 17 to 105 mm. Because both tips rise equally and only a few mm, both reach below the top of short wide objects (tuna 34, pudding 38, sugar 45, mustard 58 mm tall) and hold the vertical sides antipodally. The opening comes from two half-swings, so it exceeds the 96 mm mustard width. Added wrist mass is about 25 g, which is small next to the 0.15 N*m per 100 g budget at the shoulder.
idea.test: A jaw builder for a symmetric twin-hinge jaw: two revolute fingers, each 81 mm from its axis to its fingertip, mirrored about the gripper centreline and coupled by a gear constraint at -1:1 with each other and 1:2 to the gripper servo. Each finger takes the existing pads part (pad_angle applied symmetrically). The descent stops when the lower of the two fingertips reaches table clearance, and the fixed-jaw-face assumption in the contact checks has to be replaced by the second hinged face. Then run all 21 groups, especially dice (17 mm, each face about -15 deg bottom-in) and potted_meat_can (squeeze check at 20 N).

iterations.notes:
Iteration 12: the catalogue has run out for this failure, so this proposal is an idea that can't be tried in the simulator. It gains no group this round, and the only part to buy is 4 MR63 bearings for $3.60.

**Why the catalogue can't fix it.** All four failing objects are wide and short, and they fail the same way. Only the moving jaw swings, so at wide openings its fingertip sits well above the fixed one:
- Fingertip rise: +18 mm at 75 mm, +28 mm at 85 mm, and about +33 mm at the 90 mm pudding width.
- Face tilt: 32 to 42 deg off parallel at those widths.
- Widest opening: 91 mm, less than the sugar box (92) and mustard bottle (96).

The jaw ends up pressing on the top corner instead of the side.
- **Pads:** six parameter-only trials gained nothing. A thinner TPU skin opened the jaw to about 94 mm and still missed the 90 mm pudding box, so a wider opening alone is not enough.
- **Prismatic jaw:** tops out at 58 mm and would lose five held objects.
- **Parallelogram jaw:** rises +49 mm at 85 mm, worse than now.
- **12 V servos:** refused, since they cost $68 against $40 left. They also don't change the geometry.

The only pad settings never trialled are lip, groove and width. I didn't try them because the failure reports put the moving fingertip at the box's top edge, so a hook at the fingertip has nothing below the top to grab.

**What's new in this idea.** The six ideas recorded so far all keep the rigid fixed jaw and try to straighten the moving one. This one makes the closing symmetric instead. The fixed jaw is replaced by a mirror hinged jaw, and a printed gear pair drives both jaws from the gripper servo at 2:1.
- Each jaw turns only about ±20 deg, so both fingertips rise the same few mm and neither lifts above the other.
- Each face tilts at most about 15 deg.
- The opening goes past 100 mm.
- Squeeze stays about 20 N, so the heavy objects already held (soup and meat cans, 349–370 g) keep their grip margins.

**Risks.** Every held group assumes the fixed jaw is a vertical plane, so all 17 need re-checking. The small objects (dice, marker, wood cube) would meet two faces tilted bottom-in by about 12–15 deg. The gear ratio must be 2:1; a 1:1 coupling would halve the squeeze.

**Cost.** 4 MR63 bearings ($3.60, 3 days), about 32 g PLA plus 1 g TPU (about 170 machine minutes), and M2/M3 screws already on hand. This fits the $40, 7-day and 595-minute limits. Testing it needs a builder for a two-hinged, gear-coupled jaw in the simulator.

The tip arrives at or above the box top (contact +18 to +23 mm from the centre with the top at +19 to +23) and presses down at 74 to 88 deg. The widest opening, 91 mm, is also below sugar's 92 mm and mustard's 96 mm.
proposals.principle: A contact holds only if it reaches below the object's top and its normal is horizontal and opposed to the fixed face. A finger that swings on a circle rises by R(1-cos q) and tilts by q. Only a mechanism that cancels both the rise and the tilt as a function of the jaw angle removes the mechanism. Re-aiming the face (pad_angle) or lengthening it (reach) only moves where it goes wrong.
proposals.hypothesis:
The catalogue and the record have both run out. Six pad-only trials gained 0 groups: angle 25, 28, 30 and 45, reach 8, 16 and 30, and TPU 0.5. Reach lost potted_meat and apple to force_limit, and angles of 30 deg or more lost 5 to 12 small-object groups. The brief rules out the swaps. Prismatic tops out at 58 mm. Parallelogram link 90 opens to 96 mm but rises +49 mm at 85 mm. The 12 V servos are refused ($68 against $40 left) and would not address geometry anyway. No catalogue part keeps the narrow-object behaviour and also lowers the tip at wide openings.

New here, and different from the six recorded ideas: keep the stock hinge, and therefore every held small-object grasp, and add a cam-compensated pad. The moving pad rides a short slide on the moving jaw. A follower bearing on the pad carriage runs in a slot cam fixed to the gripper body, whose profile is exactly R(1-cos q). Below about 0.4 rad (openings under about 38 mm) the cam is flat, so the pad sits where today's pad sits. Above that, the pad descends by the hinge's rise, so the tip stays level with the fixed fingertip at every opening.

A second follower on a pivoted pad plate runs in a second slot and counter-rotates the face by the jaw angle minus the angle at 35 mm. This keeps the face vertical, within about 2 deg, from 35 to 95 mm.

The slide is inclined 15 deg outward-down, so the roughly 35 mm drop at full opening also moves the pad about 9 mm outward. That raises the widest opening from 91 to about 100 mm, enough for the 92 mm sugar box and the 96 mm mustard bottle with side clearance. It also stops the start-pose collision behind rva000 tuna's force_limit at t=0.02 s.

Squeeze stays about 20 N because the lever from the hinge barely changes. That gives 2 x 0.5 x 20 = 20 N of friction for the 5 N sugar box, and 2 x 0.4 x 20 = 16 N for the 4.2 N mustard. For the arm: 0.41 + 0.15 x 5.14 = 1.18 N*m, under the 1.62 N*m stall.
risks: The held wide objects (apple 75, gelatin_box 73, banana 70, tomato_soup_can 68, tennis_ball 66) were tuned with today's tilted, raised contact. A level, vertical contact should hold them better, but tomato_soup_can (349 g, friction 0.35) and potted_meat_can (57 mm, 370 g) depend on the squeeze staying about 20 N. The lever change is under 5%, so they should survive.

Rolling objects (apple, lemon, plum, racquetball, tennis_ball, golf_ball, strawberry) are held at the equator. With the tip lowered to fixed-jaw height, both contacts now sit low and could push the balls up. The 20-deg pad today partly aims at the equator, so these may need System 1 to raise the grasp. No groove is added, to keep the small objects unchanged.

Small objects (dice, large_marker, wood_block_cube, flat_screwdriver) see no change below about 0.4 rad if the cam's flat dwell is accurate. Backlash in the slot could let the pad drop about 1 mm, but that is below the TPU skin's compliance.

idea.name: cam-compensated drop pad on the stock revolute jaw (inclined slide, two-slot cam keeps the tip level and the face vertical)
idea.description: The stock hinged jaw is unchanged. A pad carriage on two 3 mm rods with LM3UU bushings rides a slide inclined 15 deg outward-down on the moving jaw. An MR63 follower on the carriage runs in a printed slot cam bolted to the gripper body, beside the hinge. The cam profile is flat for jaw angles up to about 0.4 rad, then drops the carriage by 81(1-cos(q-q0)) mm, which cancels the fingertip rise. A second MR63 follower on a pivoted TPU-skinned pad plate runs in a parallel slot, offset about 12 mm, and turns the face back by the jaw angle, keeping it vertical. For openings under about 38 mm (dice, marker, wood block, screwdriver) the cam is flat and the pad behaves exactly like today's 20-deg pad. For wide openings the tip stays at fixed-jaw height and the face stays antipodal, and the maximum opening grows to about 100 mm.
idea.test: Simulator builder needed: a revolute jaw whose pad frame gets a jaw-angle-dependent offset and rotation. Use dz(q) = -81(1-cos(q-0.4)) for q > 0.4 (else 0), dx = dz*tan15deg outward, and face rotation -(q-0.36) for q > 0.36, all as a kinematic coupling to the gripper joint. Add 22 g at the moving jaw. Then re-run all 21 objects with System 1 re-tuning.

proposals.result: idea recorded, not tested: cam-compensated drop pad on the stock revolute jaw (inclined slide, two-slot cam keeps the tip level and the face vertical); it would need $5.70 from the manifest, 3 days, 98 machine min; within the budget left

iterations.notes: I made no params or swap move this time. The record shows no pad value gains a wide object, and the brief shows the swaps are worse: prismatic tops out at 58 mm, parallelogram link 90 rises +49 mm at 85 mm, and the 12 V servos are refused on budget. Another pad trial would only repeat failed ones. If a builder ever exists, the idea to build first is this cam-compensated pad. It needs no change to the stock hinge, so the 17 held groups keep their kinematics below about 38 mm. It costs about $6.90 bought (2 x LM3UU at $1.20, 1 rod at $1.50, 2 x MR63 at $0.90), 3 days of lead time and about 98 machine minutes, all within budget. It is the only recorded idea that both opens past 96 mm and keeps the face vertical at every opening.
